newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Columbia CEO devising game plan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Columbia CEO devising game plan.

text.p: Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp chief executive and chairman Dr. Thomas Frist said Tuesday he intends to compile a game plan for the embattled hospital giant over the next seven to 10 days.

That plan will be submitted for review to the U.S. Justice Department, possibly along with a request from the company for 90 to 100 days to implement the plan, Frist said in an interview with Reuters.
"We need to put together a game plan over the next seven to 10 days that we can present to Justice first so that they're not hearing it piecemeal up there," Frist said.

"My goal is to get in here, assess the landscape as quick as possible, come up with a really carefully thought-out, meaningful action plan, present it to them ... ask for further comments or suggestions from them, ask for 90 to 100 days to fully implement that plan and gain their confidence," he said.
He added, "I hope .. we could bring this to a conclusion much quicker than one, two years."

A patrician Southerner with a long history in the healthcare business, Frist, 58, was elevated from vice chairman to chief executive and chairman of the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company on Friday.

He replaced long-time CEO Richard Scott, who resigned, along with president and chief operating officer David Vandewater, under the cloud of a spreading federal investigation of the Nashville, Tenn.-based company.

Frist said he is "very serious" about questions concerning the ethics of Columbia's practice of offering equity interests in certain company-owned hospitals to physicians that refer patients to those hospitals.
The company recently brought in additional counsel to advise on the issue and moved to halt such physician syndication deals, Frist said.

"There were several in the works. In spite of all this high profile, my predeccessor had continued on that line," he said. "We said that we would not only stop them, but I would go through a thoughtful process of unwinding those."

The company is also halting an aggressive and costly national advertising campaign started under Scott, Frist said. "I don't see at this point us moving forward on the same aggressive style of national branding," Frist said.
"We ought to go back to...our roots and have the message delivered for a particular community about the assets of that hospital and build that image up," Frist said.

In getting oriented, Frist said he was a third of the way through with interviewing Columbia's six group presidents. He said the talks would help him know who can best take the company forward. "A good many of them are right here internally because this is a situation of urgency," he said.
"I should fall back on a few, one or two, key people external to the company who have been tried and proven with me in the past. It's important to have some new faces," he added.
He declined to discuss rumors that Columbia has been in or has put on hold merger talks with Santa Barbara, Calif.-based Tenet Healthcare Corp, the second-largest for-profit U.S. hospital company.

He said the company is focused on dealing with the government probe, enhancing shareholder value, improving patient care and making internal changes so that Columbia can "have our growth through internal growth for a while."
That said, he added, "As a publicly held company, if somebody approaches us, we must consider it."
He said a company name change is not being discussed, as has been reported elsewhere.
"That is not under consideration now," he said.
((--Chicago Newsdesk 312-408-8787))
